planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained, sandy or chalky soil in full sun; Adriatic crocus flowers appear with the foliage rather than before it.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained, sandy or chalky soil in full sun; Adriatic crocus is native to Greece and bears white flowers with a yellow throat and striking orange-red stigma lobes in October, opening alongside its foliage rather than before it like many fall crocus. It naturalizes readily under turf or in a rock garden on soil that stays on the dry side through summer dormancy. Once established it multiplies slowly by offsets and self-seeding in congenial conditions, needing little care beyond good drainage.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in dry, stony or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Boryi crocus blooms over a long season from September into December.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in dry, stony or sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Boryi crocus is native to western and southern Greece and Crete, where it grows on dry stony or sandy ground, producing large creamy-white flowers with a many-branched orange style over an unusually long fall-to-early-winter bloom season from September through December. It suits a rock garden or raised bed where its need for sharp drainage and a dry summer rest can be easily met. Leave the foliage to die back naturally in spring to recharge the corm for the following season.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Niveus is among the latest and hardiest of the fall crocus species, often blooming into November.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Niveus crocus bears one of the largest flowers of any fall crocus, white to pale lilac with a yellow throat and bright red styles, opening in November, among the latest and hardiest autumn-flowering crocus species available. It is traditionally found growing wild in Greek olive groves, tolerant of the light cultivation and seasonal dryness found there. Plant it in a sunny, well-drained site and let the strap-like foliage die back naturally in spring before the next dry summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Tournefort's crocus is unusual for staying open at night and in overcast weather, unlike most crocus.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Tournefort's crocus is native to the Greek islands and bears soft lavender flowers with white anthers and much-divided orange stigmas in fall. It is unusual among crocus species for keeping its flowers open at night and through bad weather rather than closing, extending its garden display. It is cold-hardy to about 25°F, among the hardier fall-blooming crocus species, and performs well in a sunny rock garden or raised bed with sharp drainage.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Salzmann's crocus is one of the hardier fall crocus and naturalizes reliably once established.

directions: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Salzmann's crocus bears bright purple, cup-shaped flowers with a yellow-orange pistil from September through November. Though rarely cultivated compared to the showier fall crocus species, it is easy to grow and reliably naturalizes in well-drained soil, hardy to about -18°C, making it one of the hardier fall-blooming crocus available. Plant in a sunny border or rock garden and leave undisturbed to build a naturalized colony over the years.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3-4 inches deep in sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Yellow Colchicum needs moisture during active growth but a genuinely dry summer dormancy, more demanding than common autumn-flowering colchicums.

directions: Plant corms in sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; Yellow Colchicum is the only colchicum species with yellow flowers, native to the western Himalaya, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, and unusual among colchicums for blooming very early, in late winter to spring, rather than in fall. It needs reliable moisture while actively growing but a genuinely dry dormant period in summer, making it more demanding than the common fall-flowering colchicums and better suited to a rock garden or bulb frame than an ordinary border. It is genuinely scarce in commercial trade, generally available only through specialist alpine or bulb society sources.

planting.note: Plant corms in August 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade; Variegated Colchicum flowers emerge leafless in fall, like most colchicums.

directions: Plant corms in August in well-drained soil in full sun to dappled shade; Variegated Colchicum is a Mediterranean fall-blooming species whose flowers emerge leafless directly from bare ground, patterned with a distinctive tessellated or checkered texture similar in effect to a checkered fritillary. It blooms in September and October, following the same general culture as other colchicums, with strap-like leaves appearing separately in spring and dying back by summer. As with all colchicums, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where pets or children forage.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall 3 inches deep in cool, calcareous, well-drained soil in full sun; Spring Meadow Saffron blooms very early, sometimes before the ground has fully thawed.

directions: Plant corms 3 inches deep in cool, calcareous, well-drained soil in full sun; Spring Meadow Saffron produces goblet-shaped, bright pink-to-lilac flowers very early in the season, often appearing in February through April before the ground has fully thawed. Native to Pyrenean and alpine meadows up to 2000 meters elevation, it naturalizes well in rockeries and fine turf in cool climates with calcareous, well-drained soil. It is reasonably common among specialist spring-bulb catalogs and, once established, builds a long-lived naturalized patch with minimal care.

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall into well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Widow Iris needs a dry summer rest to bloom reliably, so avoid summer irrigation once dormant.

directions: Plant tubers into well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Widow Iris (formerly classified as Hermodactylus tuberosus) bears unusual, fragrant flowers with lime-green standards over nearly black, velvety falls, blooming in late winter to early spring on 18-inch stems. It needs a dry summer rest after flowering to bloom well the following year, making it well suited to a Mediterranean-style border or rock garden where summer water can be withheld. It naturalizes readily in grass or gravel once established and also performs well in containers.

planting.note: Plant corms in fall into sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; Chilean Blue Crocus is frost-tender and best grown in a container that can be kept dry and protected during summer dormancy.

directions: Plant corms in sharply drained, sandy soil in full sun; Chilean Blue Crocus bears intensely gentian-blue, goblet-shaped flowers to an inch across in February and March, native to high, dry Andean slopes in Chile. It needs sharply drained soil kept dry through its summer dormancy and is frost-tender, so in colder climates it is best grown in a container that can be moved under cover or kept in an unheated greenhouse over winter. Once a rarity verging on extinction in cultivation, it is now increasingly offered by specialist rare-bulb dealers, making it a genuine showpiece for a dedicated bulb collector.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Giant Grape Hyacinth naturalizes well under spring-blooming shrubs without becoming invasive.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Giant Grape Hyacinth resembles an oversized grape hyacinth reaching about 12 inches tall, with dark purple-to-navy, densely beaded flower spikes blooming in April and May. It is easy to grow and, unlike some Muscari relatives, is not aggressively spreading, making it a good choice for naturalizing under spring-blooming shrubs or in a mixed bulb border. It is sold by mainstream fall-bulb retailers and performs reliably with minimal care once planted.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in late summer or early fall 3-4 inches deep into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Autumn Squill is unusual among Scilla relatives for blooming in late summer rather than spring.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Autumn Squill (also sold as Scilla scilloides) is East Asian in origin and unusual among the squill relatives for blooming in late summer to early fall, in August and September, rather than in spring like most Scilla. Pink-mauve flower spikes reach about a foot tall above grassy foliage, adapting to a wide range of ordinary garden soils. It makes an interesting, easy-care late-season bulb for a border or naturalized planting where most other small bulbs have already finished for the year.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Rain is a cross of 'Purple Sensation' and Allium cristophii, combining traits of both parents.

directions: Plant bulbs 4-5 inches deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Rain is a cross between the popular 'Purple Sensation' and the star-flowered Allium cristophii, producing dense, deep-purple flower globes about 4 inches across on medium stems 20-30 inches tall. It blooms from late spring into early summer and is a good pollinator plant, drawing bees readily to its many small star-shaped florets. Like other ornamental alliums it is drought-tolerant and deer- and rabbit-resistant once established, and the dried seed heads add continued interest if left standing after bloom.
